steps.tx: An **osteochondroma**, or solitary exostosis, is the most common benign neoplasm of bone, accounting for more than thirty-five percent of all benign skeletal lesions. It originates as an aberrant cartilaginous physis sprout that herniates from the metaphysis during childhood growth. The lesion develops as a bony outgrowth capped by hyaline cartilage, typically located around the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia.
steps.say: Osteochondroma is the commonest benign bone tumor, accounting for over a third of all benign lesions. It starts when a snippet of growth plate cartilage breaks free from the metaphysis and grows outward. It forms a bone projection capped by cartilage, most often around the knee.

vis.alt: Anatomical illustration showing an osteochondroma outgrowth pointing away from the knee joint.
vis.caption: Osteochondroma emerging from the metaphysis and pointing away from the adjacent joint.

steps.tx: The pathognomonic radiographic criterion is uninterrupted **corticomedullary continuity** between the host bone and the outgrowth. On plain radiographs, the cortex of the host bone flares outward to become the cortex of the lesion, and the cancellous marrow cavity of the stalk merges continuously with the host medullary canal. The stalk characteristically projects away from the adjacent joint toward the shaft.
steps.say: The diagnostic feature on X-ray is corticomedullary continuity. The cortex and cancellous bone marrow of the lesion flow directly into the host bone without any boundary. The outgrowth always points away from the adjacent joint in the direction of the muscle pull.

vis.title: Morphological Subtypes of Exostosis
rows: Points away from nearest joint line
Higher risk of traumatic stalk fracture

steps.tx: A critical diagnostic dimension is **cartilage cap thickness**, which serves as the primary prognostic marker for secondary malignant transformation. In children, a metabolically active hyaline cap measures five to ten millimeters, but after skeletal maturity, it thins to under five millimeters. A cartilaginous cap exceeding fifteen to twenty millimeters on magnetic resonance imaging in an adult strongly indicates malignant transformation into secondary chondrosarcoma.
steps.say: Measure the cartilage cap thickness on magnetic resonance imaging. In growing kids, the cap can be up to one centimeter thick. But once bones mature, it shrinks to under five millimeters. If an adult cap measures over one and a half to two centimeters, suspect secondary chondrosarcoma.

right.title: Chondrosarcoma Transformation
points: New onset pain and rapid expansion

steps.tx: Autosomal dominant **hereditary multiple exostoses** results from loss-of-function mutations in EXT1 or EXT2 genes, which encode glycosyltransferases crucial for heparan sulfate polymerization. Patients present with bilateral, symmetric osteochondromas associated with skeletal dysplasias, including limb shortening, coxa valga, and ulnar shortening with Madelung-like wrist deformity. The lifetime risk of chondrosarcoma transformation climbs to five to ten percent.
steps.say: Hereditary multiple exostoses is an autosomal dominant condition caused by EXT1 or EXT2 mutations. Patients develop dozens of symmetric bumps across their skeleton, accompanied by short stature, bowed forearms, and ankle valgus. Their lifetime risk of malignant transformation jumps to five to ten percent.

vis.title: Solitary versus Multiple Exostoses
rows: Forearm bowing, short stature, coxa valga

steps.tx: Definitive **surgical excision** is indicated for painful neurovascular compression, limitation of joint range of motion, overlying bursa inflammation (exostosis bursata), or suspected malignancy. Surgery entails complete extra-periosteal resection of the stalk down to normal host cortex, including total removal of the cartilaginous cap and overlying perichondrium. Incomplete perichondrial excision permits residual chondroblasts to generate local recurrence.
steps.say: Excision is indicated for pain, nerve compression, restricted joint movement, or a thick cartilage cap. You must excise the entire stalk flush with the host cortex, including every bit of the cartilaginous cap and surrounding perichondrium. Leaving behind perichondrium allows the tumor to grow back.

left.title: Indications for Surgery
points: Adult growth or cap over 1.5 cm

right.title: Surgical Principles
points: Resect flush with host cortical bone

quiz.q: What pathognomonic radiographic feature confirms the diagnosis of an osteochondroma?
options: Uninterrupted corticomedullary continuity with the host bone
A sunburst periosteal reaction extending into soft tissue
A radiolucent nidus surrounded by dense cortical sclerosis
An eccentric purely epiphyseal soap-bubble lucency
quiz.explain: Corticomedullary continuity, where the cortex and medullary cavity of the lesion are continuous with the host bone, is pathognomonic of osteochondroma.

quiz.q: In an adult, what cartilage cap thickness on MRI raises high suspicion of chondrosarcoma transformation?
quiz.explain: A cartilage cap thickness exceeding 1.5 to 2.0 cm in a skeletally mature adult strongly suggests secondary malignant transformation into chondrosarcoma.
